answer: Agents can make valuable actions count only after a rotating set of peers attests that the same identity completed them across several epochs. Each peer checks signed receipts against a public atlas of prior work, while a pulse of random audits catches duplicated or fabricated claims. Because attestations require independent histories, minting fresh identities does not multiply reputation; an attacker must instead sustain many believable agents and pay the real cost of doing useful work. Even a pearl-bright fake needs time, resources, and colluding peers to pass.
